A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.

title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
summary: Agentic large language model (LLM) applications turn one user request into a sequence of model and tool calls over a growing context. Retaining this context's key-value (KV) state in GPU memory lets later calls reuse it instead of recomputing it, but at fleet scale this needs substantial memory. We characterize four production Microsoft M365 workload traces (Deep Research, Enterprise Assistant, Coding Agent and Enterprise Chat) spanning more than 121 million model calls. In Deep Research, the application issues 89% of model calls and the median context grows from about 10K to 68K tokens by the 30th call. About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache. With the public Llama-2-70B KV layout standing in for confidential models, one 99th-percentile Deep Research session exceeds the 80 GB HBM of an NVIDIA H100, and holding all live sessions at their peak needs an estimated 501.8 TB of HBM, although inference occupies only 5.6% of that retention time. Trace-driven replay shows that a one-hour idle cap cuts this ceiling by 3.6x while raising the share of calls that recompute context only from 4.07% to 4.53%. Under tighter budgets, eviction alone is insufficient: at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute and clairvoyant furthest-next-use 31%, whereas multi-resolution retention (MRR), which demotes the LRU session's KV state to int4, lowers this to 13.6%. Placement imposes a separate limit: when the next call reaches a different deployment, cached-context reuse drops from 89% to 29%, and treating KV state as deployment-local raises the recompute floor under unlimited memory from 5.4% to 20.2%. These findings motivate retention that changes the representation of KV state, together with deployment-aware routing or migration. We plan to release AgenticTraceSim, a parametric trace generator, and a residency replay framework.

title: MailRail: Mitigating Incast Congestion with User-Space, Node-Based Flow Control
comment: To appear in IA3 2026. 9 pages, 10 figures
summary: Irregular workloads, such as those stemming from Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, frequently induce severe incast congestion in large-scale parallel environments. Existing fabric-level congestion control mechanisms rely on reactive, link-level rate limiting that degrades overall throughput. While receiver-driven, credit-based flow control offers a proactive alternative, as process counts scale memory slots per rank fall below usable thresholds, rendering traditional rank-based accounting untenable. To address this challenge, we introduce MailRail, an out-of-order, asynchronous messaging framework, along with a novel user-space, node-based credit flow control system. By shifting credit accounting from individual processes to shared per-node pools, our proactive, fabric-agnostic approach maintains sufficient credit availability even as process density grows, enabling processes to dynamically utilize freed credits without waiting for receiver-side redistribution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that node-based flow control achieves up to a 1132x speedup over unconstrained execution at an adversarial incast ratio of 4096:1 while adding minimal overhead on uniform workloads.

title: QuarkShard: Decomposing Cross-Shard Requests into Single-Input Transactions
summary: Sharding blockchains enhance scalability by distributing the workload across multiple shards. Within sharding blockchains, securely and efficiently processing cross-shard user requests remains a pivotal challenge. Traditional sharding blockchain protocols execute cross-shard requests under a processing paradigm that treats each user request as a monolithic entity to preserve its atomicity, inherently introducing significant intra-shard BFT execution overhead and cross-shard communication overhead. We propose QuarkShard, a sharding protocol that breaks away from this traditional paradigm to achieve intra-shard and cross-shard overheads below the lower bounds imposed by conventional approaches. QuarkShard decomposes cross-shard requests into single-input-shard transactions, where each transaction requires consensus and processing within only a single shard, thereby substantially reducing total request processing overhead. Meanwhile, through a carefully designed request decomposition algorithm, QuarkShard guarantees fund atomicity or location atomicity during request execution. QuarkShard also enhances the security of blockchain sharding systems against MEV attacks and flooding attacks. Empirical evaluation across a wide-area network spanning four AWS regions demonstrates that QuarkShard achieves superior performance, attaining a peak throughput of $1024$k requests per second with sub-$4$-second latency. Benchmark comparisons show that QuarkShard achieves up to $210.7\%$ and $314.8\%$ of the maximum throughputs of Kronos and 2PC, respectively.

title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
summary: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
summary: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.

title: On the Power of Alternating Local Certification with Constant-Size Certificates
summary: We study alternation hierarchies for distributed decision in anonymous networks with constant-size certificates. A prover and a disprover alternately assign certificates to nodes over a constant number of rounds, after which each node decides whether to accept based on its own input and the certificates observed in its neighborhood. An instance is accepted if all nodes accept. Unlike previous work on distributed alternation hierarchies, which considered restricted local computation (Reiter, PODC 2024) or logarithmic-size certificates (Feuilloley et al., ICALP 2016), we focus on constant-size certificates and the role of neighborhood information in determining expressive power. We consider three models: SET, where nodes observe only the set of certificate sequences of their neighbors; MULTISET, where multiplicities are also visible; and PORTS, where neighbors can additionally be distinguished by local port numbers. We establish that SET is strictly weaker than MULTISET, which is in turn strictly weaker than PORTS, and that all three alternation hierarchies are strict at every level. Despite their severe restrictions, these models are remarkably expressive: LEADER belongs to the third level of SET. Our main characterization shows that, over finite input alphabets, SET coincides exactly with monadic second-order logic (MSO$_1$). Moreover, every language definable in counting monadic second-order logic (CMSO$_1$) belongs to PORTS, while MULTISET already contains languages that are not CMSO$_1$-definable. Nevertheless, this expressive power has fundamental limitations. PORTS does not capture MSO$_2$: neither Hamiltonicity nor the existence of a perfect matching belongs to PORTS. Furthermore, over unbounded input alphabets, PORTS cannot verify that every node has been given the correct network size.

title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
summary: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.

title: Scalable Levenberg-Marquardt Training Framework for Deep Learning
summary: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.

title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
comment: Accepted for publication in The 32nd IEEE International Conference on Parallel and Distributed Systems (ICPADS 2026)
summary: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.

title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation
summary: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.

title: EnterpriseSynth: Zero-Execution SFT and Evaluation Data from OpenAPI Specs
summary: Tool-using large language model agents require substantial training and evaluation data, yet collecting execution traces from enterprise APIs is often unsafe, expensive, or infeasible because of access controls, compliance constraints, rate limits, and the risk of modifying production data. We present EnterpriseSynth, a zero-execution framework that converts OpenAPI specifications into supervised fine-tuning trajectories and paired evaluation instances without invoking the underlying APIs. The framework uses a four-stage pipeline for specification parsing, intent generation, trajectory synthesis, and static validation. Each generated trajectory is checked against the source specification for endpoint, parameter, type, and schema consistency before being admitted to the dataset. We evaluate EnterpriseSynth on 17 real and synthetic APIs. Adversarial refinement increases the validator's detection rate for planted schema violations from 57-80% to 98% (43/44). Across five random seeds, a compact open-weight model fine-tuned on EnterpriseSynth data outperforms both an untuned model and a Self-Instruct baseline on held-out APIs. Performance remains consistent on five private, hand-authored API specifications that were not available during training, with tool-selection accuracy of 40.0% on the private set and 39.6% on the public held-out set. However, an independent LLM-based evaluation shows that endpoint-selection accuracy substantially overestimates end-to-end correctness: accuracy falls from 48.9% under the endpoint-level metric to 21.3% when argument selection and values are also evaluated. These results demonstrate that OpenAPI specifications can support scalable, execution-free data generation, while highlighting the need for argument-level evaluation when assessing the deployment readiness of tool-using agents.

title: Understanding LLM Hallucinations Caused by Soft Errors
summary: While hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively studied from a software perspective, limited attention has been paid to hardware-level factors. In this paper, we performed a case study to understand LLM hallucination caused by soft errors on hardware. We introduce LLMEI to inject soft errors into LLMs during inference, based on what we evaluate the impact of soft error across diverse LLM architectures and tasks, including mathematical reasoning and code generation. We summarize the taxonomy of different failure modes based on LLM hallucination behaviors and analyze their distributions under different error rates. Our find- ings underscore the hallucination-specific diagnostics within the reliability of LLM implementation on hardware.

title: ForTress: Bringing Assurance and Determinism for LLM-Driven Fortran-to-Python Translation
summary: Modernizing mature scientific software from Fortran to Python can improve accessibility and integration with modern computing tools, but manual rewriting is expensive. Large language models (LLMs) make translation more practical, yet generated code can pass regression tests while violating source-language semantics, and contextual corrections may not persist across subsequent translations. We present ForTress, which solidifies recurring LLM translation decisions into guarded executable rules for deterministic reuse and provides semantic assurance for a non-trivial subset of these rules. Its LLM-assisted auditing process expresses universally quantified preservation obligations over mechanized Fortran and Python semantics in Lean. Human experts review semantic fidelity and correspondence with production rules, and Lean's kernel checks proofs and refutations under explicit assumptions. These audit records expose the conditions either supporting correctness or identifying failure cases. We evaluate ForTress on 17 benchmarks from 15 scientific software spanning diverse domains. The translated programs achieve bitwise-identical with native Fortran on all evaluated tests under the recorded execution and initialization configurations. Against these software, ForTress accumulates 193 executable rules and 188 audit records, of which 121 have checked soundness proofs, including 31 established after counterexample-guided refinement. Cross-software reuse exceeds 90% for 14 of the 15 software. Even with additional assurance and determinism, the LLM usage cost is 44.2% lower than direct LLM translation.

title: SIEVE: A Parameterized GitHub Corpus Builder for Software Engineering Research
summary: Software engineering research increasingly relies on large, richly annotated corpora of real-world code. Still, researchers typically assemble these with ad-hoc scripts or static, pre-built datasets that offer no control over corpus composition. This leaves a gap for a reusable tool that goes below the repository level and builds annotated, function- and class-level code corpora under researcher-specified criteria. We present SIEVE (Software Ingestion & Extraction for Verifiable Evaluation), an open-source, parameterized GitHub corpus builder that, unlike repository-level mining tools, works at code granularity: it locates individual functions, methods, and classes in repositories and extracts them as records, giving direct control over corpus construction based on several criteria, including widely used programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C++), repository quality, and creation date. To support software engineering research and LLM evaluation on real-world code, SIEVE extracts CodeSearchNet- and OpenClassGen-compatible records, each annotated with 22 structural metrics and AST-derived features, and optionally with a CodeBERT-based P(AI-generated) score (F1=0.9478, AUROC=0.9902), alongside the third-party dependencies declared in each repository's package manifest. These annotations enable researchers to conduct structural analyses, investigate code dependencies, assess AI-generated code, and construct customized benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, including under temporal constraints. A manual validation of 400 records in four languages and two granularities shows 100% accuracy in code metrics and import detection, 99.0% in source completeness, and 99.5% in metadata accuracy. SIEVE is publicly available with a live demo at this https URL .

title: Enjoying the Product but Not Joining the Builders: Investigating Why Students Don't Contribute to OSS
summary: Open-source software (OSS) participation provides students with authentic exposure to collaborative, real-world software development, yet active contributions remain limited. This short paper presents an exploratory study of computing students' perceptions, knowledge, and experiences with OSS at the University of Hawai'i at Manoa. We administered a survey and analyzed 122 responses using both quantitative and qualitative methods. Students reported moderate OSS familiarity and frequent OSS use in coursework and personal projects, yet only 12.3% actively contributed and engagement with OSS communities was limited. Key barriers included skill gaps (72.89% of non-contributors), time constraints (59.81%), and codebase complexity (66.67% of contributors), often alongside imposter syndrome (36.45%). Students indicated that more time, mentorship, beginner-friendly issues, better onboarding/documentation, and curricular incentives (e.g., course credit) would most increase participation, while most reported their courses do not require or incentivize OSS contributions (58.20%). Grounded in a single institutional context, this study provides a nuanced understanding of how curriculum structure, faculty encouragement, and competing academic demands shape OSS participation. These insights inform the design of targeted curricular and institutional interventions aimed at supporting student onboarding and participation in OSS communities.

title: No One-Size-Fits-All: Adaptive Code Editing with Feature-Based Strategy Selection
summary: Large language models have shown strong potential in automating code editing (CE) tasks, yet most existing systems rely on a fixed CE strategy (i.e., one-step, search-replace, and plan-apply) across diverse scenarios. In practice, CE tasks vary widely in code context, edit locality, and semantic complexity, causing no single strategy to perform consistently well. Moreover, systematic studies on the relationship between strategies and CE tasks remain scarce, limiting further optimization of LLM-based code editing strategies. To address this gap, we construct CEBench, comprising 500 real-world CE tasks curated from SWE-bench. Then we compare three representative CE strategies (one-step, search-replace, plan-apply). Our study reveals two key findings: (1) each strategy exhibits distinct advantages for specific CE tasks, with no universal optimality; (2) strategy effectiveness is significantly influenced by four core task features: total lines of code, modification type, modification scope, and task type. Motivated by these findings, we propose Ace, an adaptive code editing framework that dynamically selects optimal CE strategies based on task features. Unlike classifier-based or instruction-prompting approaches, Ace employs a fine-tuned LLM that learns feature-strategy mappings from empirical data to recommend strategies with interpretable rationales. Extensive experiments on our CEBench-verified show that Ace outperforms state-of-the-art baselines: it boosts Pass@1 by 21.7% while reducing token consumption by 27.3% compared to the best baseline (AutoCodeRover). Our strategy selector achieves 72.6% selection accuracy with 69.9% rationale accuracy (Cohen's Kappa = 0.807), providing transparent and trustworthy decision-making for developers.

title: MergeShuffle: Reconstruct Shared Libraries for Improved Performance and Security
summary: Debloating shared libraries has been an active research topic for years. Tools for shared library debloating rely on either static or dynamic analysis techniques to discover which parts of the shared library is used. Once these parts are found, these tools take one of two routes, either removing parts of the library that are not used, requiring reconstruction of the library; or they simply overwriting the unused functions. However, recently a broad study~\cite{brown2024broad} on debloating tools has shown that some of these tools either increase the static binary size, or are generally less effective for complex workloads. In this paper, we argue that shared-library debloaters' performance can be improved by proper reconstruction of the shared-libraries once the used functions in the library are identifies. We propose \myapp, a novel tool for reconstructing shared libraries from a given set of file ranges to eliminate unused code based on user-specified requirements, without requiring access to source code. \myapp takes as input a shared library and a set of file ranges to retain, and performs a two-phase reconstruction: merging nearby ranges to reduce loading overhead, and shuffling them to minimize file size while preserving page-aligned memory mappings. The shuffling problem is formulated as a variant of the Traveling Salesman Problem and solved using a heuristic algorithm. \myapp utilizes program headers to remap retained code to its original memory addresses, preserving user-specified functionality. Our results show that \myapp achieves up to 60\% reduction in file size, 16\% reduction in memory usage, and 32\% reduction in runtime, while maintaining user-specified functionality and improving security.

title: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
summary: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) reports flag operations whose safety depends on project-specific context, and maintainers must decide which reports describe real defects. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret this context, but adjudicating a report with them requires the decisive code, which often lies far from the reported line, and a decision basis that program analysis can check. We present VulnSAGE, an adjudication system for SAST reports that connects LLM reasoning to program structure in both directions. Its report-centered slicer recovers the dependencies of the reported operation together with the program structure that explains them, such as the caller object on which a helper acts. CLAIM, an intermediate representation for report judgments, records each model interpretation as a semantic fact that cites the program relations it assumes. Program analysis checks these premises, and the verdict follows from the facts whose premises hold. Both mechanisms share a program graph, which lets the model cite the code it reads and lets the checker query those citations. Statically supported true positives then guide proof-of-concept generation and runtime reproduction. Across 187 labeled reports from four corpora covering five vulnerability families, VulnSAGE rejects 89 of 97 false alarms and retains 85 of 90 real defects. Under a common PoC procedure, 25 of its positive verdicts reproduce at runtime, compared with three for the LLM-based adjudicator LLM4SA. Applied to 45,440 alerts raised by five SAST tools on the 200 most-starred C/C++ projects on GitHub, it reproduces 104 defects at runtime. Maintainers have confirmed 24 of the 26 defects they have responded to, including ten previously unknown defects, nine of which are already fixed.

title: Efficient Program Reduction for Library Fuzzing Harnesses
summary: Library fuzzing harnesses translate generated inputs into API calls. When a complex harness triggers a crash, developers must determine whether the cause is a library defect or invalid harness usage. A smaller reproducer can simplify this investigation, but obtaining one requires repeatedly building and executing modified harnesses and analyzing their crashes, making manual or even automatic minimization time-consuming. Moreover, data-dependent statements prevent the reducer to remove unnecessary code and the heavy stack trace symbolization in libraries also slows down the candidate execution. To address these challenges, we present HarnessMinimizer, a system for efficient minimization of C/C++ library fuzzing harnesses. Its optimized pipeline reuses header analysis and prepared libraries and runtimes to reduce the work required to build and execute each simplified harness during the reduction process. It records and replays input values so that unnecessary input operations can be removed without changing the values supplied to surviving calls. It also uses a fast method to check whether each simplified harness preserves the original crash, avoiding repeated stack trace symbolization. We evaluate HarnessMinimizer with four reduction engines on 200 crash cases from 21 open source libraries. Compared with the unoptimized pipeline, HarnessMinimizer achieves speedups of 3.46-4.51 times in average total wall time. Average harness size decreases from 1,352 original tokens to 143-263 remaining tokens after minimization. In crash triage using a large language model, accuracy in identifying harness bugs increases from 28% with the original harnesses to 44-51% with the minimized harnesses, while accuracy for library bugs remains at 100%.

title: Code Skill Server: A Large-Scale Search Engine for Code Generation Skills
summary: Agent skills have proven to be an effective technique for improving agent ability on specific tasks, including software engineering, natural science, and mathematics. During such a process, using agent skills often involves manually discovering and organizing skills from heterogeneous sources, while existing skill retrieval methods mainly focus on selecting relevant skills from established skill libraries. However, with the rapidly increasing number and variety of reusable agent skills, manually searching for relevant skills across heterogeneous sources is becoming impractical at scale. In this paper, we introduce the Code Skill Server (CSS), a large-scale search engine for finding the most useful code generation skills for a target task. CSS consists of a skill server that incrementally collects and indexes publicly available code generation skills from multiple sources, with 993 skills included in the corpus used in this work. Extensive experiments across different retrieval methods and code generation benchmarks show that the best CSS configuration improves Pass@1 by up to 13.91% and consistently improves all evaluated models by at least 4.21% in the cross-model evaluation. These results demonstrate that CSS can effectively search for and serve relevant skills, improving code generation quality and enhancing models' code generation capabilities. Code and the CSS-993 corpus are available at { this https URL }.

title: Towards Agentic Proof Harness Engineering
summary: Formal verification of real-world projects requires substantial manual effort, from specifying correctness properties to constructing the infrastructure needed to check them. We envision verification agents that assist developers throughout this process. Among the many tasks involved, one stands out as both foundational and amenable to automation: proof-harness engineering. A proof harness defines an isolated verification environment for a program unit, such as a function or module, by providing symbolic inputs, initialization code, and models of its dependencies. Today, proof-harness engineering remains largely a manual task performed by verification engineers. To explore the potential of coding agents for this task, we propose an agentic proof-harness engineer that automatically constructs verifier-ready harnesses from a software project and a designated verification target. We combine the agent with formal soundness and precision guards to validate generated abstractions and guide their refinement. We evaluate the feasibility of our approach in an exploratory case study on curl and libuv, using three historical assertion violations already embedded in the source code as verification properties. Our results show that the agent successfully constructs proof harnesses that enable CBMC to detect all three violations. We further demonstrate the potential for reusing these harnesses with other verification tools.

title: MLOps-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Production ML Engineering in Real Repositories
summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to modify and maintain machine-learning systems in production, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either competition-style ML experimentation or generic repository issue resolution. We introduce MLOps-Bench, a repository-grounded benchmark for production ML engineering. Unlike prior ML-agent benchmarks, MLOps-Bench evaluates executable lifecycle changes inside real ML repositories, spanning data pipelines, feature engineering, model training, model serving, monitoring, CI/CD and governance, and end-to-end integration. Each task is grounded in repository evidence and includes a natural-language requirement, oracle patch, plausible buggy baseline, fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and provenance metadata. The benchmark contains 212 validated tasks from 31 public ML repositories, with 636 fail-to-pass tests and 856 pass-to-pass tests. We evaluate six agents and find that the best system solves 31.2% of tasks while passing 68.7% of tests, showing that current agents often make partial progress but still fail production-relevant behavioral requirements. MLOps-Bench shifts agent evaluation beyond model building and issue fixing toward repository-native MLOps work where correctness depends on lifecycle reasoning, behavioral robustness, and preservation of existing system behavior.

title: Recall-Oriented Precise Binary-to-Source Function Matching
summary: Binary-to-source function matching supports software composition analysis by identifying reused third-party code, but existing embedding-based approaches restrict subsequent refinement to initially retrieved candidates. When the correct source function is absent from this set, selecting or filtering the available candidates cannot recover the match. Inlining further complicates the retrieval by combining multiple source functions into one binary function. In this paper, we propose BScout to improve matching precision and uncover additional matches. BScout uses the positional information of existing matches to supplement candidates for unresolved binary functions, extending the search beyond the initial candidate set, and adopts composition-aware training to address the inlined composition matching. Large language models are adopted to select and review matches, while positional information also helps filter inconsistent results. Experiments show that BScout is effective in binary-to-source function matching. BScout achieves overall higher precision, recall and F1 scores than BinaryAI and SBridge with acceptable analysis costs. Particularly, on large stripped binaries, BScout outperforms the competitors with a precision increment of 32% and approximately 2.9 times the recall.

title: An Interactive GraphRAG Workspace for Reifying, Auditing, and Steering Conversational AI Memories
summary: Conversational Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely employed in software engineering for code generation, debugging, and architectural design. However, as developers engage in multi-session development tasks, technical knowledge becomes siloed in isolated, linear chat histories. Reusing context across sessions leads to three critical challenges: (1) flat-vector retrieval fails to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies between distant architectural decisions; (2) temporal drift in software packages and APIs results in silent context poisoning when reusing aged dialogue logs; and (3) raw conversation concatenation induces prompt bloat and attention degradation. We present CognitiveCanvas, an interactive tool that transforms conversational AI memories from ephemeral text logs into persistent, manipulable, and audited knowledge objects. \textsc{CognitiveCanvas} integrates: (1) a Hierarchical Semantic Fact-Graph (HSFG) that distills dialogues into Goal, Fact, and Code artifacts, achieving a 92.2\% token reduction while enabling multi-hop GraphRAG traversal; (2) a Continuous Temporal Drift Auditor coupling 60+ regex heuristics with live calendar-anchored LLM verification for 1-click self-correction; and (3) a Spatial-Symbolic Prompt Compiler (SSPC) that translates 2D direct manipulation gestures (Voronoi clustering, node resizing, synthesis edges) directly into structured attention directives

title: Empirical Insights from AI-Powered Software Engineering in Practice
summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is becoming indispensable in future software engineering. Its application spans a wide spectrum - from assisted development to autonomous software engineering, requiring organizations to address associated risks and challenges. This paper investigates these issues through three case studies, highlighting practical problems encountered during GenAI integration. Based on these findings, it provides targeted recommendations for managing risks and ensuring reliable outcomes. This paper provides guidance for effective and responsible GenAI adoption in software engineering based on empirical insights.

title: Enforcing Code Reasoning in Agentic Scaffold for More Effective Issue Resolution
summary: Reasoning is central to ReAct-based programming agents, yet whether and how they reason about code remains unclear. We study 7,955 issue-resolution trajectories from six single- and multi-agent scaffolds across four programming languages on SWE-bench-Verified, SWE-bench-Pro, and SWE-bench-Lite. We identify 12 forms of code reasoning in 66.95% of trajectories. Code reasoning is associated with higher resolution rates, and its intensity increases with task complexity. However, it remains largely unguided: agents may focus on surface-level symptoms during localization, fail to refine near-correct patches, overlook issue requirements, and generate tests with limited behavioral diversity. To address these limitations, we propose DeskCheck, an agentic scaffold that systematically guides code reasoning throughout repository-level issue resolution. DeskCheck simulates execution paths to localize root causes, simulates candidate patches to refine near-misses, audits patches against issue requirements, and reasons about corner-case inputs and expected outputs before generating tests. On 731 SWE-bench-Pro instances, DeskCheck improves resolution rates over mini-SWE-Agent and Claude Code by 6.29% to 10.53%, at an additional cost of $0.02-$0.28 per instance (average: $0.14). Per-phase analyses show higher method-level localization recall, more successful repairs of imprecisely localized issues, and better detection of missed corner cases in near-correct patches. Exact McNemar tests show statistically significant improvements across all subject LLMs (p < 10^-10), while repeated experiments support robustness to agent nondeterminism. These findings motivate systematic code reasoning as a means of improving programming agents.

title: Trust but Verify: Designing Region-Inhomogeneous Forward Dynamics for Discrete Diffusion
comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: AI for Stochastic Dynamics. 10 pages
summary: Continuous diffusion treats the forward process as a design space; discrete language diffusion often uses absorbing corruption, leaving context fully trusted throughout generation. This makes trust binary: corrupted context is copied as ground truth, propagating errors into generated spans. We reopen this design space by combining absorbing and uniform-mixing kernels with region-dependent rates. Missing positions follow absorbing dynamics, while context undergoes low-rate random substitution, exposing the model to observed but uncertain tokens during training. At inference, a heuristic sampler re-injects noise into suspicious context under an annealed intensity and freezes context updates late in the trajectory. An 8,000-step finetune of a pretrained 170M-parameter masked diffusion model takes under five hours on a 6 GB laptop GPU. The base model assigns roughly 50% probability to observed tokens even when they are uniform-random garbage. For uniform-random corruption, finetuning detects corrupted context with 0.96 recall and 0.91 precision, improves infill token-F1 by 3.8 points at 10% corruption and 6.4 points at 20%, and removes the accuracy dip next to corruptions. Clean conditioning shows no measurable regression, with a false-edit rate below 0.4%. Gains for plausible corruptions are weaker: about 0.5 F1 points at 10% corruption, without statistical significance. Our results suggest that detectability and damage depend jointly on departure from the data conditional: nearby noise is hard to detect and semantically mild, while distant noise is conspicuous and destructive. We interpret absorbing diffusion as the infinite-contrast limit of a trust axis, analogous to the signal-to-noise gap between known and unknown regions in diffusion inpainting. In our setting of a 170M model and a single text domain, intermediate trust is reached by changing forward dynamics rather than architecture.

title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents (TTCL). 15 pages, 2 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at this https URL

title: CGDT-CESN: Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network for Multivariate Time-Series Prediction
summary: Accurate prediction of multivariate time series requires models that simultaneously capture variable-specific dynamics and cross-variable interactions. In this work, a Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network (CGDT-CESN) is proposed, which comprises a modular reservoir architecture with each cluster distinctly specializing in one of the variables in the multivariate time series. An innovative reservoir design is proposed in which inter-cluster connections are enabled by empirically observed correlations among variables, providing a data-driven coupling mechanism. Apart from conventional readout training, inter-cluster connection weights informed by correlations are trained, which in turn allows the reservoir to capture time-varying cross-variable dependencies without sacrificing computational efficiency and further improves forecasting accuracy. The prediction performance of CGDT-CESN is found to be superior to that of the conventional ESN when evaluated on two fundamentally different datasets: Twitter information cascade evolution and solar wind forecasting. Also, the improvement in performance is preserved across multiple prediction horizons, even when presented with a low volume of data. By unifying cluster-specific specialization with learned inter-variable coupling, CGDT-CESN offers a principled, data-driven route to multivariate time series prediction.

title: BOLT: Multi-Bottleneck Bound-Guided Learning for Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling with Time Lags and Resource-Coupled Transport
comment: 12 pages main text plus 18 pages of supplementary material appended after the references (30 pages total). Code, data, and trained models: this https URL . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
summary: Flexible job-shop scheduling becomes resource-coupled when a scarce vehicle fleet moves jobs between stations, because the schedule sets the transport waits. BOLT (bound-oriented learning for transport-coupled scheduling) builds a lower bound from chain, machine-capacity, and fleet-capacity relaxations. The bound equals the makespan at termination, so its per-step changes form a reward that sums to a constant minus the makespan. Because it never exceeds the attainable makespan, each candidate's bound increase is a proven rise of the makespan floor, which the policy reads as a price. The root bound certifies a completed schedule's suboptimality gap without a solver. On industry-motivated 10-module prefabricated-construction instances, explicit transport coupling outperforms a transport-penalty policy in every tested cell where loaded moves occupy at least 66% of fleet time and in none at or below 56%. Across five zero-shot 50- and 80-module production batches, BOLT outperforms the best dispatching-rule pair on four and the penalty policy on the three with long moves. In the three-vehicle 80-module batch, its mean makespan is 13.0% below the best pair and 4.2% below an hour-budget constraint-programming solver whose proven gap averages 34%. BOLT decides in 2.3-5.9 ms per event on one processor core and re-plans a disruption in seconds.

title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
summary: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield's Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems.

title: CF-NODE: Counterfactual Spatial Node Intervention for Test-Time Adaptation Under Domain Shift, Evaluated Across Five Diabetic Retinopathy Datasets
summary: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.

title: Rank Measures of Fine-Tuning Updates Need a Noise Baseline
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Under review at TMLR
summary: Studies of what fine-tuning does to a language model often summarise the weight update $\Delta W$ by its rank. We compare the rank measures used for this against the same measures on a random matrix of the same shape, and against two harder references: the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content. Measures that count directions put our fine-tuning updates only a little below noise; stable rank, computed from the same singular values, puts them far below. Both are right: an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds for thirteen released pairs up to 8B parameters, and it is not a mark of alignment: with training held fixed, instruction data does not stand out from Wikipedia or code, DPO gives the same update whether its preference labels are real or half swapped at random (one model, modest preference strength), and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update of all. Applied to a recent claim that post-training is superficial because the effective rank of the weights barely changes, the baselines show that a random update of the same size leaves that rank almost unchanged while wrecking the model, and that an edit built on the effective rank of the update has no measurable effect in our tests. Rank measures of weight updates need a noise baseline, and claims about alignment need a control without alignment content.

title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards
summary: Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards, with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Lean4AgenticRL**, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. **Lean4AgenticRL** first builds a *problem-specific workflow* system that balances the agent's own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using **Lean4AgenticRL**, we train **LAR-9B/27B**, a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of similar size. **LAR-27B** achieves **77.3%** on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by **9.89%** and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by **5.07%**. These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.

title: Generative Value Classifier
summary: Q-learning is premised on learning a function to predict the value of a state-action pair, with the goal of using such a function to guide policy improvement. Most approaches learn this function from scratch using scalar or distributional return targets. This discriminative approach leaves another source of supervision for learning representations unused: the actions themselves. Rather than directly predict the return of a state-action pair, we ask the reverse question: how likely is the action under each possible return? This perspective provides a critic whose generative component is a return-conditioned policy, which can share the actor's architecture. Training this policy supervises the critic with every action rather than with returns alone, and a squared-error loss anchors the critic's Q-value to the bootstrapped target. We evaluate our approach on both offline and online RL tasks and show gains over leading discriminative methods, including distributional RL methods.

title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ($D$) and error-step KL contrast ($\Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by $\Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$ also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.

title: Learning smooth dynamics via Kinematic Interpolants
summary: Inferring dynamics from real-world experimental data is inherently ambiguous, as many plausible dynamical systems can explain the same positional observations at measurement times. For higher fidelity modeling of applications ranging from single-cell RNA to vortex dynamics and even flocking of birds, scientific observables increasingly also include velocity estimates that serve to resolve this issue. However, incorporating this rich information in a scalable manner, free of simulation or unnecessary approximations, has remained a difficult challenge. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Interpolants (KI), a novel framework that extends the seminal methodology of stochastic interpolants to infer nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, i.e., observables with position and velocity measurements. Empirically, we demonstrate that across several scientific datasets, KI achieves superior reconstruction of the underlying dynamics compared to existing baselines while requiring only a fraction of the training time.

title: Don't Retrain, Remix: Adaptation of Web Agents using Mixture Hypernetworks
summary: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
comment: Preprint, project page: this https URL
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92-100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M-parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block-diffusion verification approaches either assume $T=0$ or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree-based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled-noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared-Gumbel-noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: this https URL

title: Deterministic Bounds on Accuracy and Stability of Metric-Space Regression and Classification
summary: Data-driven approaches often face ambiguity in datasets due to sensor or target noise, insufficient information, and noise in the input data. While best-fit machine learning methods can accommodate such noise through uncertainty estimates, they are prone to overfitting and it is challenging to quantify ambiguity of the relation between inputs and targets. We introduce a geometric framework that quantifies this ambiguity through the average kernel size, computed with data-dependent, i.e. model-independent, feasible sets derived from worst-case input and target noise. The framework provides computable, deterministic, non-asymptotic bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy for a finite, constructed dataset, independent of the predictive model class, and applies to regression and classification with pseudo-metric input spaces and metric target spaces. The ambiguity of the input-target relation implies three consequences: an empirical error floor, an accuracy-stability trade-off, and, under standard probabilistic assumptions, a strictly positive distribution-training error gap when training below the accuracy bounds. Under standard Borel assumptions for Euclidean norms, the distributional analogue of the average kernel size is related to Bayes risk as it reduces to the optimal distribution root-mean-squared error times the square root of two. Experiments spanning tabular regression, image regression and classification datasets yield nontrivial bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy on a constructed dataset, alongside descriptive comparisons with model performance on the original datasets. The bounds provide a computable, model-independent reference scale on the constructed dataset and comparisons with model performance on the original dataset are descriptive.

title: Coverage Cliffs in Off-Policy Quantile Certification
summary: We study when logged contextual-bandit data can certify an upper tail quantile for a policy selected from the same sample. We construct a PAC-Bayes Bernstein lower-confidence envelope for the target cumulative distribution function (CDF), simultaneous over a predeclared threshold grid and all data-dependent posteriors. The resulting procedure, TailCert, uses the envelope's first crossing of level p to return an atom-safe upper confidence bound on the selected posterior's pooled p-quantile (or inconclusive). It can also be used to select a policy under a certified tail constraint. The concentration ingredients are standard; the main theoretical contribution is a matched finite-class certification boundary comparing full logs with their joint weighted CDF indicators at a fixed threshold. On an explicit rare-action class, the required sample size grows linearly with the overlap factor W, logarithmically with policy-search and confidence complexity, and quadratically with the inverse CDF safety margin; the upper and lower bounds agree up to constants in the stated regime. On this class, the CDF reduction hides which actions exceeded the budget; retaining action counts restores the full-log rate. Simulations verify the predicted search-complexity shift, winner's-curse failure of naive reuse, and the power cost of splitting.

title: Structure-Aware Spatial Kernels for Gaussian Process Distributed Port-Hamiltonian Systems
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproduction scripts are available at this https URL
summary: Gaussian process distributed port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-dPHS) enable data-driven modeling of distributed dynamical systems while preserving their physical structure. However, standard stationary kernels can be inefficient for spatially heterogeneous systems because they neither exploit known input invariances nor reflect structured spatial dependencies. We address this limitation with a structure-aware kernel design that removes irrelevant state coordinates and decouples state and spatial dependencies through a tensor-product covariance. This modular construction allows qualitative knowledge of spatial heterogeneity to be incorporated by selecting an appropriate spatial kernel without requiring an analytical description of the underlying profile. Numerical experiments on a nonlinear string with periodic, smoothly varying, and semi-piecewise stiffness profiles demonstrate that structural decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, while profile-matched spatial kernels yield substantially larger gains in force-field and trajectory reconstruction.

title: Noise-Robust Forced Alignment for Spontaneous Speech
summary: We show that forced aligners degrade on spontaneous, noisy real-world speech, and that fillers, laughter, and disfluencies corrupt word boundaries, impacting many downstream applications. We revisit the classical GMM-HMM aligner with upsampled WavLM features instead of MFCCs, explicit phone units for fillers and non-lexical vocal events trained on verbatim-annotated spontaneous speech, and a discriminative projection fitted on clean and noise-corrupted feature pairs to improve robustness. The pipeline is self-bootstrapped from 149h of curated audio without manual or external boundary targets. On conversational (Buckeye) and disfluent (FluencyBank) speech it reaches word-boundary MAEs of 20.6 and 76.9ms, 19% and 17% lower than the strongest of ten baselines. Catastrophic misalignments (>200ms) are 2.7 times rarer than Montreal Forced Aligners (MFA) best model even after widening MFA's search beam, which we show removes a large pruning artifact from its conversational error; event units halve the error next to laughter, while being meaningfully more robust than existing aligners.

title: Initiating Removal from Operational Symptoms in Federated Vehicular Networks
summary: Connected vehicles train a driving model through federated learning (FL) and drive with it, so a faulty contribution often surfaces only as a delayed symptom on the road. Federated unlearning (FU) assumes that a removal request names what to forget. A symptom names no vehicle or round, and aggregation has already spread its cause across the fleet. We propose \underline{A}ggregation-\underline{T}ime \underline{O}perational-evidence \underline{N}eutralization of \underline{E}ffects (\method{}), which makes unlearning a term of the FL aggregation rule. \method{} projects everyday driving errors and reported symptoms onto a subspace spanned by recent global increments. It propagates the surviving effect of every contribution with curvature estimated from these increments and scores all contributions in one backward pass. A two-tier correction suppresses suspected effects in every round and eliminates confirmed ones after a one-round probe. We prove that backward scoring matches forward scoring and that the elimination is exact when training is flat outside the subspace. On three driving datasets, \method{} leaves 43\% to 61\% less residual harm than the strongest baseline in eight of nine settings while staying within 0.36 points of full retraining in utility.

title: Flat Loss, Evolving Features: Grokking in Modular Addition
comment: 97 pages, 17 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Can a network keep learning while its training cross-entropy stays nearly flat at a positive level? We show that it can. On modular addition, a standard testbed for grokking, ReLU networks trained with supported-Polar hidden updates, normalized output-layer updates and weight decay can keep 100% training accuracy while their hidden features change and held-out accuracy rises from zero to above 90%, at relatively flat training cross-entropy. Correct classification need not minimize cross-entropy, which still depends on prediction confidence. We prove this coexistence for one-hidden-layer networks in two finite-window theorems from constructed initializations: one gives a constant gain in the Fourier fraction of the hidden features, and the other holds at arbitrarily low positive loss, where a readout refitted on the training data generalizes before the network. Experiments from random initialization show the same coexistence on a window fixed in advance, and in deeper networks held-out accuracy also rises over post-hoc windows with a net increase in training cross-entropy. With a last-layer rate set per training fraction and head decay scaled with the prime, deeper networks at p=47 and 61 meet a criterion on post-hoc windows, fixed in advance, in nearly all fresh runs. A one-block transformer trained with the same updates and a slowly decaying output gain keeps every training pair correct at every logged checkpoint while its training cross-entropy rises and its held-out accuracy approaches one; with two blocks this holds through the held-out rise, after which training pairs begin to flip. A plateau in training loss need not be a plateau in learning. Code: this https URL .

title: Diagnosing GNN Failure Modes with Layer-Wise Probe Entropy
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically evaluated only at their final layer, obscuring how task-relevant information evolves during message passing. We introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that freezes a trained GNN, fits an independent linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy alongside normalized predictive entropy. Across real and synthetic graph settings, layer-wise probe entropy distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, a capability not demonstrated by existing geometric measures. Moreover, by comparing shallow and deep models, we show that the onset of entropy degradation separates the two main GNN failure modes: structural mismatch under heterophily, which appears from the earliest layers even in shallow models, and excessive-depth oversmoothing, which emerges only as propagation depth increases. These results establish probe-entropy trajectories as a tool for analyzing information flow in GNNs and motivate future work on adaptive depth selection and early-exit mechanisms.

title: Rarity of Singletons Matters & Supplementary Materials
comment: supplementary for the main paper has been added as well
summary: Estimating missing-mass and unseen-species counts from finite samples relies heavily on rare-event occupancy statistics, particularly singletons. In small-sample regimes, these statistics can be highly variable, making classical estimators sensitive to sampling fluctuations and potentially unreliable. We propose a fragility-aware (FA) framework that explicitly quantifies this sensitivity and adaptively regularizes conventional missing-mass and unseen-species estimators. Using singleton-based fragility measures derived from probability mass and occupancy counts, we formulate an entropy--Kullback--Leibler (KL) optimization that adjusts the reliance on base estimates according to their fragility. The resulting objectives are strictly concave, admit unique closed-form solutions, and require no Poissonization or asymptotic approximations. The framework provides a lightweight correction to classical estimators, including Good--Turing and Good--Toulmin, while reducing reliance on potentially unstable rare-event statistics. Across 360 experimental configurations spanning synthetic distributions and real-world language corpora, our method remains competitive in stable regimes while improving estimation accuracy and stability in fragmented, long-tailed, and small-sample settings. The findings demonstrate that accounting for the fragility of rare observations can improve the reliability of inference about unobserved species and their associated probability mass.

title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models
summary: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. Our key contribution is $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler, an optimizer that reconciles these objectives by embedding a stochastic sampling-and-annealing step as a noisy quantizer inside a first-order $\Sigma\Delta$ noise-shaping loop. The loop pushes noise from weight quantization, high-order frustration, and mini-batch sampling out of the low-frequency adaptation band, so that discrete weight updates follow the smooth descent trajectories embedded in the rugged loss landscape. We validate the framework on a planted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) benchmark with a known minimizer; on CIFAR-10, where a $13$M-parameter ternary model comes within $1\%$ of full-precision accuracy; on ImageNet-1k, where a ternary ResNet-18 comes within $0.4\%$ Top-5 accuracy of a ternary baseline; on class-incremental continual learning, where prior-task accuracy is preserved; and on MatMul-free language models up to $2.7$B parameters, where it outperforms a straight-through-estimator baseline under matched continued pre-training. Compared with standard quantization-aware training, $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler reduces the training memory footprint by over $50\%$, delivers an order-of-magnitude speed-up, and reduces weight-update memory traffic by four orders of magnitude, making it attractive for on-device training and fine-tuning of large binary and ternary models.

title: Understanding Stability of Outer Nesterov Momentum on Stochastic Pseudo-Gradients
summary: Large neural networks are commonly trained across many workers, and communication between them is a major cost. Workers therefore take several local optimization steps before sending their net parameter displacements, or pseudo-gradients, to an outer optimizer, which often applies Nesterov momentum. We study how the outer momentum, the number of local steps and the averaging over workers control the training dynamics, and in particular their stability. For random quadratics, we derive an exact mean-square stability criterion in any dimension, which reveals that the inner batch size determines whether increasing the number of local steps eventually stabilizes or destabilizes the outer iteration. Moreover, while averaging the pseudo-gradients of independent workers can make larger outer momentum values admissible, the number of workers required for stability can grow exponentially with the number of local steps. Finally, we show that the mean-square dynamics governing stability can be probed directly at intermediate neural-network checkpoints using shared-minibatch perturbations. We test our theoretical findings across networks, and measure their consequences for training loss.

title: Alert-List Concordance for Evaluating Imputation Strategies in ICU Sepsis Prediction
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 14th Workshop on Data Mining in Biomedical Informatics and Healthcare (DMBIH 2026), held in conjunction with IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: Preprocessing is an under-measured reliability risk in clinical prediction: a model can keep a similar AUROC and still change who receives an alert. Imputation quality is commonly evaluated using reconstruction error or aggregate discrimination, neither of which directly measures agreement on which patients are flagged. At a matched alert rate, pipelines with similar aggregate performance can produce different patient lists. This question is especially relevant under the frequent, structured missingness of real ICU records. We therefore introduce alert-list concordance, which asks whether two pipelines identify the same high-risk patients, measured by the Jaccard similarity of their top-k% alert sets with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. On PhysioNet/CinC 2019 (40,336 patients, 71.9% missingness), we compare nine imputation strategies and a native-missingness baseline using a fixed XGBoost configuration, fitted and Platt-calibrated separately for each strategy. After Bonferroni correction, 22 of the 28 reconstruction-method pairs showed no statistically significant difference in patient-level AUROC, yet their alert lists overlap at Jaccard 0.518 to 0.750. Similar aggregate discrimination can therefore accompany different patient selections. ForwardFill is a separate outlier, pairing higher discrimination with the lowest overlap in the matrix, 0.40 to 0.45.
