To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

title: Steering beyond Language: Improving Multilingual Training-Free Text Embeddings via Paired-Residual Subspace Removal
summary: While deriving text embeddings directly from frozen LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, existing methods focus almost exclusively on English, leaving multilingual settings largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multilingual training-free text embeddings in LLMs. Our analysis reveals a language-conditioned embedding geometry in which semantically equivalent sentences remain misaligned across languages. We hypothesize that language-specific variation can be disentangled from semantic content to improve embedding quality. To this end, we propose Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention that steers LLM representations toward a more language-invariant semantic space. PRSR first constructs paired residuals from multilingual parallel sentences to capture language-specific deviations. It then estimates layer-wise low-rank subspaces from these residuals and suppresses the corresponding components in the last-token hidden states. We conduct more than 200 monolingual evaluations across 18 languages using MTEB and MMTEB, along with cross-lingual bitext mining between English and over 200 other languages. Empirical results demonstrate that PRSR consistently improves the performance of existing training-free baselines in both monolingual and cross-lingual settings across different LLMs.

title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.

title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
summary: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
summary: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.

title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
comment: 37 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Socius. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

title: Social Bias or Social Desirability? Comparing Factorial Survey Experiments for Humans and Large Language Models
summary: Factorial survey experiments are a survey method from the social sciences that uses descriptions of socially complex situation (``vignettes'') to elicit judgments such as social bias. They provide two major benefits: (a), they reduce the effect of social desirability inherent in self-reported social biases, and (b), they make it possible to separate the effects of multiple sociodemographic attributes. These aspects are also desiderata for the evaluation of social bias in LLMs, but are often ignored in social bias evaluations. In our study, we evaluate social bias in humans and eleven LLMs on the basis of four different English and German factorial survey experiments. Our results show that the LLMs mirror the human biases only partially and sometimes even invert them. We provide evidence that this is due to a fundamental difference in how humans and LLMs react to socially complex situations. While such vignettes reduce social desirability bias in humans, this is not the case for LLMs, where the alignment-induced tendency towards socially desirable responses carries over directly. We therefore caution against applying bias measurement techniques from the social sciences that were developed for human to measure attitudes and bias in LLMs.

title: Beyond What Is Visible: Context-Aware Sentiment Across Online Communities Among Crisis Events
summary: Social media offers timely insight into disaster experiences, yet online communities may not represent those affected on the ground. Uneven participation can bias crisis information systems toward data-rich locations and obscure communities with fewer digital traces. We address this with an adaptive cross-community learning framework that combines text and aggregate mobility signals with socioeconomic and hazard-informed community representations, supplementing sparse local observations with evidence from structurally related cities. We evaluate the framework on the January 2025 Southern California wildfires and 2024 Hurricane Helene in Florida. The adaptive model achieves the highest F1-score in both cases (0.5923 and 0.7615), while augmentation has its strongest effect where original observations are limited. The framework also reveals finer cross-city community-level sentiment variation and stronger sentiment-mobility correspondence than text-only models, with relationships differing across disaster contexts. These findings support crisis systems that better account for context-dependent evidence and improve interpretation of underrepresented community signals.

title: Generative AI Produces and Transmits Beauty Bias
summary: Societies reward people judged to be attractive by standards intertwined with gender and race. In this paper, we examine if and how generative AI may contribute to these dynamics. We audited 27 text-to-image generators released between 2022 and 2026 using simple prompts that never mention attractiveness or beauty, analyzing 51,300 generated faces and 160,196 photographs of real people across primary and supplementary comparisons. We used three automated measures and collected ratings from 550 human raters on a subset of images. Nearly all generators produced faces scoring above photographed faces under automated measures, and human raters judged the outputs of all 23 generators as significantly more attractive than photographed faces, even after correction for multiple comparisons. When focusing our analysis on gender, we find that 37% of female-prompted generated faces outscored the median professional fashion model. Across racial, ethnic, and national categories, groups associated with darker skin tones tended to receive lower attractiveness scores than groups associated with lighter skin tones. In a preregistered hiring simulation experiment (N = 570), exposure to AI-generated faces selected for high human-rated attractiveness lowered hireability and trustworthiness ratings and reduced interview advancement for an identical test set of candidates paired with photographs of real people; exposure to retouched photographs produced no such effect. Generative AI can reproduce racial hierarchies and gendered patterns of beauty and alter the context in which real people are judged.

title: Regulating for an AI Commons: Adopting, sustaining, and defending people-first innovation trajectories
summary: Technological principles of openness, interoperability, and decentralization are integral to building an AI economy that is accountable to the public and truly responsive to local needs and constraints. However, Big Tech's firm control over essential elements of the stack (such as chips, cloud, models, data, and talent) limits valuable alternatives from reaching the scale necessary for sustained growth. Worse still, hyperscalers continue to enclose and extract value from publicly funded and volunteer-driven technologies without adequately distributing these returns. We see consolidated power within a few entities and "enshittification" of once-transformative innovations. Embedding ethical micro-level tools (like open data repositories or small-language models) into workflows is promising, but without a consistent innovation strategy, they also often end up perpetuating and being appropriated by the same exploitative trajectories. Instead, this whitepaper outlines a three-pillared holistic and intentional policy approach that i) actively pushes for the adoption of cooperative technologies in existing and emerging systems, ii) sets up collective institutional structures to sustain and maintain them in the long-term, and iii) introduces regulatory proposals that limit private entities from disempowering them through uncontrolled enclosure and extraction. Through desk research and purpose-specific case studies, we argue for the importance of such an approach in the Global South, where structural constraints around infrastructure, financing, and policy governance make it difficult for AI commons and cooperative AI tools to emerge and survive. The paper concludes with key open questions for campaigners, policy advocates, researchers, and grassroots organizers to consider and explore while working towards peoples' solidarity within and between Global South countries.

title: Evaluating Predictor-Corrector Dependence in Hard-Constrained Climate Emulators
summary: Climate emulators often enforce physical constraints by correcting each state predicted by a neural network, but evaluating only the corrected forecast conflates predictor skill with the effect of the correction. We introduce an evaluation framework that separates these contributions by comparing corrected forecasts, pre-correction predictions along corrected trajectories, and autonomous rollouts with correction disabled. We further cross correction during training and inference to distinguish its immediate effect from how it shapes the learned predictor, and use matched nonphysical controls to test whether improvements are specific to the physical correction. In ACE2, correction substantially improves physical consistency. In a three-seed ACE2 pilot, models trained with correction produce less accurate uncorrected precipitation forecasts at short horizons than models trained without correction, but more accurate forecasts at 10 and 30 days. This contradicts our preregistered hypothesis that the deficit would grow with forecast horizon. In a separate nine-seed experiment, directly supervising the uncorrected output reverses its precipitation forecast deficit at 72 hours while maintaining the accuracy of corrected forecasts at 24 hours. In ConCerNet's heat-equation system, projection-trained models have higher uncorrected trajectory-based vector-field RMSE than models trained without projection, while restoring the physical projection recovers accuracy far more effectively than a matched nonphysical control. Together, these results show that hard corrections can reshape the predictors trained alongside them, creating dependencies that are not visible from corrected forecasts alone. Hard-constrained emulators should therefore be evaluated by separately measuring predictor accuracy, correction effects, and their interaction during training.

title: GCAM-Gym: A Benchmark for Agent-Based Climate Policy Search
summary: Comparing climate-policy search methods requires accounting for differences in policy control, available observations, feedback timing, and simulator budgets. We introduce GCAM-Gym, a Gymnasium-compatible environment that supports full-policy evaluation and stepwise control through a common interface and exposes the components of the policy objective. We compare seven search and control systems in three settings: target attainment and cost, cost-temperature trade-offs, and one-step delayed feedback. Each system is evaluated with ten seeds per setting, for a total of 3,210 attempted GCAM evaluations. Four systems share a budget of 24 attempts per seed; among these, CMA-ES achieves the highest interquartile mean (IQM) of the best returns from completed policy evaluations in all three settings. We release the evaluation archive and analysis tools to reconstruct the reported comparisons without running GCAM.

title: Water-Energy-Data nexus reveals sustainability gaps and priorities for AI infrastructure
summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on interconnected water, energy, and data systems spanning infrastructure life cycles and diverse geographies, with the potential to intensify water and energy insecurity, exacerbate social inequities and lead to cascading sustainability issues globally. Yet assessments commonly examine them separately, limiting our understanding of where resource pressures arise, how they are transferred across space, and who bears their consequences. To address these challenges, we established a water-energy-data (WED) nexus framework that captures the spatial and life-cycle dependencies of AI infrastructure, and use large language models to synthesize 12,825 water- or energy-related studies across four resource-intensive AI infrastructure activities: mineral extraction, semiconductor manufacturing, data center operation and electronic-waste processing. The evidence map identifies a mismatch between the interconnected activities supporting AI infrastructure and boundaries used to assess them. Researchers assess operational energy more than water use and other indirect demands, while interactions across locations and life-cycle activities remain understudied. These gaps obscure how resource demands shift among infrastructure nodes and regions, and how data-enabled benefits compare with their underlying costs. The WED nexus provides a foundation for integrated assessment of spatially metacoupled systems, while the evidence map can inform priorities for managing the sustainability implications of the AI boom.

title: A Large Language Model LLM Approach to COVID-19 Fake News Detection
summary: Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

title: Jev-as-a-Judge for Brazilian Portuguese Information Retrieval: Relevance Assessment and Reranking
summary: This study investigates Jev, a System One model designed for fast, structured decision-making, in information retrieval. We use Jev-as-a-judge to generate relevance judgments for four Brazilian Portuguese IR collections covering different domains and compare them with the official relevance judgments of each collection. We also evaluate Jev as a reranker. For relevance assessment, exact agreement ranged from 52.9% to 64.9%, while quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.52 to 0.82. Most disagreements involved adjacent relevance levels, with at least 94.5% of annotations matching exactly or differing by only one relevance level. Despite differences at the individual query--document level, Jev-generated qrels produced similar retrieval system rankings, with Kendall's tau ranging from 0.90 to 0.93 for NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus across the two evaluation metrics. For reranking, Jev reordered the top 1,000 BM25 candidates for each of the 50 Quati test queries, increasing nDCG@10 from 0.3329 to 0.6331 (+90.2%) and MRR from 0.6852 to 0.9033 (+31.8%). These findings support Jev as a relevance assessor and show improved ranking effectiveness over BM25 in the evaluated reranking setting.

title: LSNR: Learned Sparse News Recommendations with Attentive User Modeling
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Accepted at SIGIR-AP 2026
summary: Current learned sparse approaches for recommender systems, such as STAR, represent a user by concatenating their interaction history into a single query string. For news, this creates two bottlenecks: concatenation collapses a user's distinct reading interests into one flat query, and, because news articles are long-form text, concatenating several news articles quickly overruns the context window of the language model used as backbone and forces quality-degrading truncation. To address both bottlenecks, we introduce learned sparse news recommendations (LSNR). LSNR encodes each article independently and constructs a sparse user vector by combining learned, attention-based weighting of the per-article sparse representations with a dense-projected expansion at the user level. Experiments on the MIND and EBNeRD datasets show that LSNR significantly outperforms STAR, with these gains holding even in short-history settings where truncation is not a factor. Compared to state-of-the-art dense recommenders, LSNR is competitive in standard settings and it outperforms them when the user history is short. An ablation of the user encoder confirms that learned attention-based aggregation outperforms simpler pooling alternatives. Beyond effectiveness, an additional advantage of LSNR is that it serves from an index an order of magnitude smaller than an uncompressed dense baseline.

title: Humanity's Last Choice: A Common Evaluation Standard for Generative Engine Optimization
comment: 19 pages, 2 figures. Project website: this https URL
summary: Humanity's Last Choice describes the idea that the last choice people need to make is which AI system they entrust with the decisions that follow. These systems rely on external sources that content providers can edit through generative engine optimization (GEO) to increase source visibility and influence recommendations. Choosing among these systems therefore requires comparable evidence of how well they carry out user requests when exposed to GEO. Benchmarks have made progress in standardizing tasks, models, and metrics, but they often define their own spaces of GEO strategies and use different editing constraints. These differences can conflate gains from better optimization algorithms with those from greater freedom to edit sources, while making evaluation coverage difficult to compare across benchmarks. We therefore call for a common evaluation standard and propose a meta-taxonomy that describes where sources are edited, how they are edited, and what signals those edits target. Drawing on representative literature, we map existing strategies into a searchable space and outline a protocol for controlled comparisons with explicit coverage reporting. This provides a foundation for common leaderboards that can inform which systems people choose to rely on.

title: An improved randomized algorithm for finding sinks of Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations of the binary hypercube
summary: Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations (AUSOs) of the binary hypercube form an elegant abstraction of various optimization problems, ranging from linear programs whose feasibility region is a combinatorial hypercube, to 2-player turn-based stochastic games (2TBSGs) in which one of the players has two actions from each one of its states. The currently fastest known randomized algorithm for finding the sink of such AUSOs is the Random-Facet algorithm of Kalai (STOC 1992), and of Matoušek, Sharir and Welzl (SoCG 1992), adapted to the binary hypercube by Gärtner (RSA 2002). The expected number of vertex queries made by the algorithm is at most $e^{2\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the dimension of the cube. We design an improved randomized sink-finding algorithm that performs an expected number of only $e^{\sqrt{(2+o(1))n}}$ queries. This is the first improved bound for the problem in over two decades. The improved algorithm is obtained by adapting improved versions of the Random-Facet algorithm for solving general linear programs, and LP-type problems, developed by Kalai (STOC 1992), Gärtner (FOCS 1992), and by Hansen and Zwick (STOC 2015). The improved bound is not implied by these much more general algorithms. A key feature of the improved algorithm and its analysis is its simplicity. The structure of binary AUSOs enables a simpler description and a much simpler analysis of the adapted algorithm. In particular, the recurrence relations bounding the complexity of the algorithm depend on only one variable, and not two, and they can be solved using fairly straightforward techniques.

title: Improved Pass Complexity for Semi-Streaming Matching in General Graphs via Budgeted Price Approach
summary: We present a simple deterministic semi-streaming algorithm that computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum matching in general graphs in $O(1/\varepsilon^{2})$ passes. This matches the pass complexity of the auction algorithm of Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan~[SOSA'21] for bipartite graphs, and answers Open Question~2 of Assadi~[SOSA'24 \& TheoretiCS'25]. Our approach, which we call the \emph{budgeted price approach}, is very different from the previous $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$-pass semi-streaming algorithms for $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of matching in general graphs and improves their pass complexity. All previous approaches are augmenting-path-based and use $O(1/\varepsilon^{19})$ passes by Fischer, Mitrović, and Uitto~[STOC'22], $O(1/\varepsilon^{6})$ passes by Mitrović, Mukherjee, Sankowski, and Sheu~[ICALP'25], and $O(1/\varepsilon^{4})$ passes by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi~['25].

title: Competitive Online Clustering with Movement Cost
summary: We study the problem of online clustering with movement cost, which generalizes the fundamental $k$-server problem. At each time step, the algorithm is given a set of points in a metric space and must choose $k$ cluster centers. The cost incurred is the sum of the clustering cost at each time step and the total distance that the centers move over time. Prior work established competitive algorithms for the case $k\in\{1,2\}$ on the line metric with the $k$-median clustering objective; under the $k$-median objective, this problem is also known as facility reallocation. We substantially generalize these results to arbitrary $k$, general metric spaces, and a broad class of clustering objectives. Specifically, we consider clustering costs defined as a norm of the distance vector from points to their nearest center, which subsumes the $k$-median, $k$-center, and (square root of) $k$-means objectives, and provide an asymptotically optimal $O(k)$-competitive randomized algorithm against adaptive online adversaries. The algorithm is based on a reduction to the $k$-server problem, establishing a tight connection between the problems. In this reduction, $k$-server requests are generated by Poisson processes, whose arrival rates evolve in continuous time and are driven by a dual representation of the clustering costs. Our method of using Poissonization in this context may also be of independent interest. We demonstrate another use of the idea by deriving similar reductions for batched set chasing problems. We also consider a different family of clustering objectives defined as a norm of the vector of cluster radii, which subsumes the sum-$k$-radii and the $k$-center objectives, and give a tight $O(k)$-competitive deterministic algorithm on the line.

title: On the Metric Distortion of the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem
summary: We study the metric distortion of the minimum spanning tree (MST) problem when numerical edge weights are unavailable and each vertex reports only a ranking of the other vertices induced by these weights. We first show, through a simple example, that without assumptions on the weights, no ordinal algorithm guarantees a finite approximation ratio. We therefore focus on general metrics and present a Borůvka-inspired algorithm using only ordinal comparisons that achieves distortion $O(\log n)$. We complement this result by showing that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, no deterministic ordinal algorithm guarantees distortion at most $3/2-\varepsilon$ on all finite metric instances. We then investigate more informative settings in pursuit of constant distortion, first considering two well-studied metric classes. For tree metrics realized on the given vertex set, a more careful variant of our initial algorithm achieves distortion~$1$, recovering an optimal MST from ordinal information alone. For the broad class of doubling metrics, a different algorithm based on \emph{endpoint cut stability} achieves distortion $2^{O(D)}$, where $D$ is the doubling dimension; this is constant for fixed $D$, independently of $n$. Finally, we study a query-based extension allowing comparisons between two edge lengths without revealing their numerical values. For general metrics with $n\geq2$, fewer than $n$ edge-comparison queries suffice to achieve distortion at most $2\log_2^* n-1$, which is near-constant even for very large inputs.

title: Online geometric matching and segments block points
summary: Given a sequence of online points in general position in the plane, the geometric matching problem asks to match as many points as possible, subject to segment crossing constraints. We initiate the study of online geometric matching with limited crosses. In the $k$-crossing model each matched segment is allowed to have at most $k$ crosses, where $k=0$ corresponds to the online noncrossing matching model for which Bose et al. proved that Greedy is an optimal deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio of $2/3$. In the triangle-free-crossing model no three matched segments are allowed to pairwise cross each other. Interestingly, we show in both cases the performance of Greedy does not improve by allowing crosses, and in fact, becomes worse in the $k$-crossing setting for $k\ge 1$. In the triangle-free-crossing model, we propose a simple two-layer-Greedy deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio $4/5$. More interestingly, we propose and study the underlying segments blocking points extremal problem, and discuss its connection to vertex cover numbers and Ramsey numbers, with interesting open problems that might be of independent interest. We revisit the noncrossing model. We give a randomized algorithm which is an asymmetric version of Kamali et al., improving the competitive ratio from $0.66952$ to $0.67034$. We also show, via a conceptually simple construction, that no randomized algorithm can match more than $6/7$ fraction of points, improving the previous $16/17$ by Boyar et al.

title: Critical-state algorithms for lot sizing with all-units discounts and variable inventory bounds
summary: We study deterministic single-item lot sizing with all-units quantity discounts, linear holding costs, and time-varying end-of-period inventory bounds. Unit prices may vary arbitrarily over time. For one common positive discount threshold, we give an exact algorithm requiring $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations and $O(n^2)$ working space, including recovery of an optimal purchase plan. The method combines a critical-state theorem in cumulative-purchase coordinates with two prefix-minimum scans per dynamic-programming layer. The structural argument accommodates downward price discontinuities and distinguishes prescribed from free terminal inventory. With a fixed global set of $m$ positive threshold values, the bounds become $O_m(n^{m+2})$ time and $O_m(n^{m+1})$ space. Period-specific thresholds admit the same exact construction, but its state set can be exponential. For commensurate flow data, an inventory-lattice implementation takes $O(PW)$ time, where $P$ is the total number of price tiers and $W$ is the largest inventory-lattice width. We also derive a conditional optimality certificate from a monotone one-threshold relaxation; this certificate does not imply a near-linear worst-case algorithm for arbitrary prices. Exact-arithmetic implementations are checked against exhaustive inventory dynamic programs and tier-enumeration linear programs. An illustrative timing study identifies settings in which the lattice implementation is preferable.

title: Simpler Algorithms for Capacitated $k$-Median with $(1 + ε)$-Violations Using New Inequalities
summary: We revisit the capacitated $k$-median problem, focusing on constant-factor approximation algorithms with either $(1+\epsilon)$-cardinality or capacity violations. Previous results [DemirciL16, Li16} achieve an $O_\epsilon(1)$-approximation with $(1+\epsilon)$-violations via complex extended configuration linear programming formulations with the round-or-cut framework. We propose a simpler, unified round-or-cut framework that handles both cardinality and capacity violation settings. Our main technical contribution is a mechanism that directly utilizes the costs of local instances to generate valid inequalities. Specifically, we partition the metric space into local pieces of size $O(1/\epsilon)$ as in previous work, and construct instances of capacitated clustering with penalties, which allow client demands to be unserved at a penalty cost. Solving these local instances yields lower bounds on the original LP cost, yielding valid LP constraints. In contrast, previous approaches rely on complex extended configuration LPs over connection variables $x_{ij}$'s and opening variables $y_i$'s. As a secondary contribution, our approach achieves an improved running time of $\text{poly}(n, 1/\epsilon)$, bypassing the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$ required to solve the previous extended configuration LPs. Instead of solving the local instances optimally in time exponential in $1/\epsilon$, we obtain $O(1/\epsilon)$-approximate solutions in $\text{poly}(n, 1/\epsilon)$ time. Finally, for the cardinality-violation setting, our algorithm opens a set of at most $(1+\epsilon)k$ $\textit{distinct}$ facilities, and thus gives a bicriteria approximation in the $\textit{hard-capacitated}$ setting. In contrast, the algorithm of [Li16] may open the same facility multiple times.

title: Power of Conditional Sampling on Hypergraphs
summary: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a $d$-uniform hypergraph with $|V|=n$ and $|E|=m$. Estimating $m$ from uniformly random hyperedge samples requires $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$ samples by a birthday-paradox argument. We investigate the power of conditional sampling through a hierarchy of oracles: for an integer $1\le s\le d$, given pairwise disjoint subsets $X_1,\ldots,X_s\subseteq V$, the $s$-colorful oracle returns a hyperedge chosen uniformly at random from all hyperedges contained in $X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_s$ that intersect every $X_i$, provided one exists. For $s=1$, this samples a uniformly random hyperedge induced by $X_1$. For every $1\le s\le d$, we give a randomized algorithm that outputs $\widehat{m}\in[(1-\varepsilon)m,(1+\varepsilon)m]$ with probability at least $2/3$ using $O_{s,d}(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n))$ conditional samples, where the exponent of $\log n$ is an absolute constant independent of both $s$ and $d$. Conditional sampling thus yields an exponential separation over uniform hyperedge sampling. We also study the decision version, in which the oracle only reports whether a qualifying hyperedge exists. For every $1\le s<d$, we prove that any algorithm using the $s$-colorful decision oracle requires $\widetilde{\Omega}_{s,d}(n^{\frac{d-s}{d-s+1}})$ queries. Hence, for $s<d$, access to uniformly random witness hyperedges (random certificates) is exponentially more powerful than existence queries. For $s=d$, decision queries alone achieve $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ query complexity, but the exponent of $\log n$ is known to be $\Theta(d)$. The colorful hierarchy thus exhibits a phase transition at $s=d$: for $s<d$, random certificates are essential for polylogarithmic-query estimation, whereas at $s=d$ decision queries suffice, yet random certificates still provably reduce the exponent of $\log n$ from $\Theta(d)$ to an absolute constant.

title: Deterministic Global Minimum Cut Using $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ Cut Queries
summary: Finding a global minimum cut in an unweighted graph is a fundamental task in the cut-query model. While there exists a randomized algorithm for this task using $\tilde O(n)$ queries, known deterministic algorithms use $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ queries. We improve upon this result and give a simple deterministic algorithm that finds a global minimum cut using $\tilde O(\min\left\{ n\delta,n^2/\delta \right\})$ cut queries, which equals $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ in the worst case, where $\delta$ is the minimum degree of the graph. The key ingredient in our approach is an efficient maximum $s,t$-flow algorithm, for the case when the minimum $s,t$-cut has value at most $\delta$.

title: Approximating the Girth of an Undirected, Weighted Graph for Larger Approximation Factors
summary: The girth of a weighted undirected graph is defined as the length of a shortest cycle in the graph. In this paper, we give a randomized $O\left(m^{1+2/(k-1)} n^{1/(k-1)}\right)$ algorithm to approximate the girth of a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges to within a factor of $k$ for any real $k$. We assume that all edge weights are non-negative. For sufficiently high approximation factors, our algorithm outperforms the state of the art by polylogarithmic factors. Specifically, for approximation factors $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ where $c>5$, our algorithm gives a runtime of $O\left(m (\log n)^{5/c}\right)$, while instantiating the previous best $k$-approximation algorithms with $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ yields a running time of $O\left( \frac{cn (\log n)^{2 + 4/(3c)} }{\log \log n} + m\log n\right)$ (Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams, arXiv:2607.00938 ). Furthermore, the algorithm presented here is conceptually simple, has relatively small constants, eschews single-source shortest path and sparse spanner algorithms, and employs a new technique, which we call ``random filtering.'' That being said, the basic algorithm returns only a numerical estimate for the girth, rather than a witness cycle.

title: Dynamic Load Balancing under Restricting Updates
summary: We study the problem of load balancing in the dynamic setting. The input is a bipartite graph $G = (J \cup M, E)$ of jobs $J$ and machines $M$. Every job has a positive weight $w(j)$. The goal is to assign every job in $J$ to an adjacent machine in $M$ so as to minimize the maximum machine load, where the load of a machine is the sum of the weights of the jobs assigned to it. Although load balancing has been studied extensively in many models of computation, the only previous result in the dynamic model addresses the \emph{incremental} setting, where updates take the form of edge insertions and job deletions [BKS23b]. The authors show a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for incremental \emph{fractional} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/\epsilon)$ update time; they point out that their techniques do not extend to the decremental setting. Main Result: We obtain an algorithm which maintains a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate solution to the fractional load balancing problem under edge deletions and job insertions in $\tilde{O}(\log (n), 1/\epsilon)$ update time. Our techniques are very different from those of the incremental algorithm of [BKS23b]. Instead, our algorithm is inspired by a load-balancing algorithm from the {\sc congest} model of computation [ALPZ21]. We develop a novel analytic framework for this algorithm, which allows us to show that it performs well in the dynamic setting. Rounding Scheme: We also present a black-box rounding scheme for dynamic load balancing. Plugging in our fractional algorithm, we obtain a decremental algorithm for $(2+\epsilon)$-approximate \emph{integral} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/\epsilon)$ update time. We also obtain the same bounds for incremental load balancing by plugging in the fractional algorithm of [BKS23b].

title: Polytope Sampling at the Speed of Isoperimetry
summary: We give faster algorithms for sampling from the uniform distribution over a polytope. Our main result is an algorithm that, when applied to a polytope with $m$ constraints in $n$ dimensions, uses $m \cdot \mathrm{poly}\log(\frac m \delta)$ iterations, each running in time $O(mn^{\omega - 1})$, to return a sample within total variation distance $\delta$ to the uniform distribution. When $m =O(n)$ and $\delta = \mathrm{poly}(\frac 1 n)$, our runtime improves upon all prior works by an $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ factor. Our sampler is based on the recent \emph{functional stochastic localization} framework of [GST26], and achieves an iteration count nearly matching the Poincaré constant of the uniform distribution with respect to the logarithmic barrier.

title: Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals
summary: We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming $n$ and $k$ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $O(k^3 \log^2 k \log^4 n)$ colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed $k \geq 3$, and is better than a known lower bound of $\Omega(\log^{k-1} n)$ colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed $k \geq 6$. In addition, assuming $n$ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$. For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms.
